q-70064:
When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m\times n$ to $n\times m.$

So, since $L$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, the transpose ${L}^{T}$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix.

q-11462:

So, since $C$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, the transpose ${C}^{T}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix too.

q-20435:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a+3b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $3b.$ So, we first draw the vector $3b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/f67af4512a7ab61f862932a60dafc25ef62bc46335b7d7df323fe889f8728e6b.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $3b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=\frac{1}{2}|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=\frac{1}{2}a.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =3b+\frac{1}{2}a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a+3b=\frac{1}{2}a+3b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =\frac{1}{2}
$$

q-120244:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=a+\lambda b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $a.$ So, we begin with the vector $a,$ and then find the remaining vector needed to reach the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/0c785e189beebb0a803bceba272db156af6d3b47c690ee9527876f77c65d1891.png)

Note that in $△OAC,$ we have:

- $AC=2|b|$

- $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $b$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{AC}=2b.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC} \\  & =a+2b.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=a+\lambda b=a+2b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $b,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =2
$$

q-120260:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a-3b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $-3b.$ So, we first draw the vector $-3b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073957/assets/2484cf9fdda85c5c516babe6814f34c369ebdd91d6f100f0ce0fe4102e3c90a6.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $-3b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=3|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-3a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =-3b-3a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a-3b=-3a-3b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-3
$$

q-338004:
Suppose we have a second-order linear ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The equation is homogeneous if $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$ If it is not homogeneous, then it is inhomogeneous.

With that in mind, let's examine each option.

- The equation

$$
\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{″}-2x{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

is $\text{homogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$

- The equation

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}=x
$$

is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=x,$ which is different from zero.

- Writing the equation

$$
{y}^{″}-xy+4x=0
$$

in the form $a{y}^{″}+b{y}^{′}+cy=f,$ we have

$$
{y}^{″}-xy=-4x.
$$

This equation is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=-4x,$ which is different from zero.

q-338082:
Suppose we have a second-order linear ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The equation is homogeneous if $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$ If it is not homogeneous, then it is inhomogeneous.

With that in mind, let's examine each option.

- The equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=x
$$

is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=x,$ which is different from zero.

- The equation

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡(x){y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-6y=0
$$

is $\text{homogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $x.$

- Writing the equation

$$
{y}^{″}-(x+2)y+5x=0
$$

in the form $a{y}^{″}+b{y}^{′}+cy=f,$ we have

$$
{y}^{″}-(x+2)y=-5x.
$$

This equation is $\text{inhomogeneous}$ since, for the right-hand side, we have $f(x)=-5x,$ which is different from zero.

q-130991:
Suppose we have a second-order inhomogeneous ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is constructed by replacing $f(x)$ with zero:

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=0
$$

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

q-65019:
Suppose we have a second-order inhomogeneous ODE given in the form

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=f(x).
$$

The associated homogeneous equation is constructed by replacing $f(x)$ with zero:

$$
a(x){y}^{″}+b(x){y}^{′}+c(x)y=0
$$

Therefore, in our case, the associated homogeneous equation is

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+{x}^{3}y=0.
$$

q-339256:
If a second-order differential equation for the function $y(x)$ is given with two conditions specified at the *same* location in the domain of $y,$ then this is an **initial value problem**.

Let's go through each equation in turn.

- The first system is an initial value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the same location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=0$).

- The second system is not an initial value problem. It contains an equation only. No conditions are specified.

- The third system is not an initial value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$ and $x=4$). This is a **boundary value problem.**

q-1091:
The minor of ${x}_{21}=-2$ (second row, first column) is the determinant of the remaining entries when the column and row containing $-2$ are removed: 

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}∗ & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & ∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & 0 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the minor of ${x}_{21}=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 11\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 11\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot 11-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-33-0 \\  & =-33.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1094:
The minor of ${y}_{13}=9$ (first row, third column) is the determinant of the remaining entries when the column and row containing $9$ are removed: 

$$
Y=[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & 9 \\ 7 & 1 & ∗ \\ 0 & -1 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the minor of ${y}_{13}=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 0 \\  & =-7-0 \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$
